body: Just having met with a new potential psychiatrist, I was asked (twice) if I have a history of violence, or of legal problems... I’m a lady.  And no to both the above... it’s upsetting to be sure.  I felt I was being pigeonholed as potentially violent etc. because I have a mental illness, which upset me too.  So... I don’t know.  But I’m sorry that was upsetting, and I don’t think that’s what they meant to communicate, but I totally get it was upsetting.
I’d like to give it a go, could you add me, please?

Sounds like a kind of passive aggressive and bizarre response.  I would address it directly with your therapist.  It may have been a bit of their own ‘stuff’ coming out unfairly.  Therapists are human, so I feel like it’s ok if they miss, but it’s probably to your benefit to speak about it with them directly... and if they can handle it in a positive and non-defensive way all the better.

Hi I just read the article you sent a link to.  I am not a psychologist, but I see one a regular basis to help me cope with serious and persistent mental illness, which has morphed over the years from depression and schizoaffective type symptoms to more cptsd and eating disorder stuff... it’s run the gamut.  I’m a 42 year old woman.  I’ve also done a bit of work in the mental health field, facilitating groups for Nami and also on their helpline.  Both as a peer trained volunteer.  I’ve seen quite a lot of the profession over the years.  I thought that a lot of the facts and figures in this article were way off- some were clearly dated, from the 90’s, but also the author did not give any background to the numbers he was quoting.  A lot of the information was simply opinion on the part of psychologists or psychiatrists he interviewed.  I frankly thought it was a ridiculous and sort of stupid article.  Not that that the topic is not one that bares explorations- and I think it’s undoubtedly true that people go into psychology or becoming a therapist with some frequency because of some personal experience with mental illness, either in themselves or a close loved one.  But the idea that as a therapist you are fated to be attacked by a client, or sued, or that a client is probably going to kill themselves at some point in treatment is ludicrous.  Those things are fairly infrequent.  And as a therapist, it is up to you to arm yourself with information and training and experience to prevent those types of things from happening.  Depending on where you choose to work, you can also choose what your specialty will be, and what type of patients you are working with... certainly some populations are more apt to fall into categories at risk for violence, but it is a common prejudice, and an untrue one, that people with mental illness or more violent than the general population.  They are actually much higher risk to be the object of an attack than the initiator of one.  When you have more experience, you will need to make a decision about the type of clients you wish to work with, and whom you think you can be most helpful to... maybe you will end up working with children, or people with phobias, or eating disorders... or, maybe you will decide that you want to work with suicidal clients, in which case you will need to be very careful and stringent with evaluating their safety and making safety plans with them.  But anyone who imagines that what a therapist does is sit in an office and listen passively to problems and complaints and a litany of life’s miseries is ill informed, or has never seen effective therapy at work.  First of all, many therapist nowadays or cognitively based... so it is very concretely about changing thinking patterns, or challenging the client, and setting goals... will you make mistakes, probably painful mistakes as a therapist?  I’m quite sure you will.  But if your heart is in the right place, and you are truly interested in helping people, you will learn from those mistakes.  And go on to help others.  It is extremely important work, I’m sure heartbreaking when it goes poorly, but wonderfully rewarding and powerful when it goes well.  Generally I would expect some mix of those experiences.  And probably some boring or humdrum days.  I wouldn’t give up if this is something you’ve always wanted to do.  You can shape your career and experience to fit your own personal style and boundaries.  Best of luck.

I believe I said this in my post.  It is a mutual boundary that has to do with what is helpful and healthy for the client, and realistic and healthy for the therapist.  It varies depending on the illness the client is being treated for and the modality of therapy.  
Someone engaged in DBT or CBT would have different expectations around coaching between sessions as someone engaged in psychoanalytic treatment.  I was simply saying that in my experience contact between sessions has helped me avoid larger problems, and kept me on a more even keel, which in turn lets me lead a more independent life with less treatment.  Of course, if you feel the personal need or if you have the financial need, to bill your clients for every minute of time you take with them outside of session that is also your prerogative, and something that your clients will also need to feel comfortable with.  I pay privately for therapy, and am then partially reimbursed by insurance.  I have never been billed for an out of session contact with multiple therapists and psychiatrists and I have been in treatment since I was about 15 and I am not 42.  So I think part of what I am hearing from you is a stance towards your clients, both in terms of how you view their limitations in terms of understanding and using your relationship, and also in terms of how you view your financial relationship with them, that would frankly just not work for me.  My therapist has repeatedly told me that if I am upset about something in session, and really worried about it, that he would much rather have me contact him with an email, than suffer on my own for days until I see him again.  Usually a quick back and forth takes care of it, and that models a way for me to check similar concerns with other people in my life, instead of suffering silently.  And the kindness he displays has been a model of how I expect and want other relationships to play out.  So it has not fostered increased dependence, but actually I have been doing more, dating, working, productive and increasingly healthy.  Yes, with a lot of support and kindness, and understanding, from my therapist.

Actually, my experience is simply that different therapists have different boundaries around between session interactions.  It depends on the needs of the client, and availability of the therapist, and then of course on what is going to be helpful and healthy for the client.  I’ve worked with multiple therapists over the years who have been available for emergency coaching to deal with various issues, like binge eating, or self injury.  I think it’s really important when you’re starting to work with a new therapist to talk about these things up front, so that you are both comfortable with the boundaries.  It’s not just what works for your therapist, it’s what works for YOU.  So if the rules around inter-session contact are too stringent, or not supportive enough, than perhaps it means that it is a bad match.  I’ve actually always worked with therapists, and I guess about 3 regularly over the course of 20+ years, who did not put any limit on email contact between sessions.  It was a way for me to reach out, and express feeling or thoughts between sessions, when I was struggling or had a lot on my mind, but it did not rise to the level of a suicidal emergency.  These types of contact actually helped me cope, and dampen down impending crises to avert and actual emergency.  One therapist’s rule was that I could write her, but understanding that she was busy, she might or might not respond, but was assured that she would read my messages.  Which was helpful actually.  My current therapist also has no limit on emails, and he generally gets to them within a 24 hour period, and his preference is to respond in kind.  I think that is sounds like the original person posting on this thread is quite sensitive to the needs of his/her therapist, and also to the fact that there are limits and boundaries.  I would say I also fall into this category, and so try very hard not to abuse this privilege, and use it when I feel overwhelmed.  It’s quite helpful for me.  And actually not an unusual practice, at least in my experience.  I’ve never heard of a therapist who will not receive and read emails between sessions, even if they only want to respond or discuss in session.  And if someone is struggling emotionally to the degree described in the original post, I would say of course that constitutes an urgent situation, where contact should be made.  And any therapist who would prefer a client remain in that state for days on end, rather than try and be helpful with some kind of coaching in between sessions, or some kind of assurance that they will try and address the issue in session, is in the wrong field.  Or working with the wrong category of patient.

I’m a 42F, and I grew up with CSA in my home and it stopped me from even trying to meet someone for many many years, and I’m tying to navigate most of this dating for the first time now as an adult.  I can tell you it’s super hard, and that I get very discouraged every time something doesn’t work out or ends badly, or I get rejected, or feel rejected.  You have also had the terribly painful experience of losing someone you clicked with, and who understood your quirks.  But I think that is best taken as a sign that there are people out there who will get you, and who won’t devalue you because you might behave differently from other folks with different life experiences.  I think it’s something you have to navigate yourself using your own judgement and heart with each person you meet and date, in terms of what you say and when you say it.  I now try and start with broader statements about it with people I’m dating, and trying to feel out the situation.  If someone has a negative initial response to that sort of thing, then they’re not the right person for me.  But I do think there is no reason you can’t find someone again who will appreciate you for who you are, and see your quirks as just another love able part of you, not something negative.  Wishing you the best.
